q-revolutionen-27#explanation: The US Constitution was adopted in 1787, the Declaration of the Rights of Man followed in 1789, the abolition of slavery in the French colonies in 1794 and the Code civil in 1804.
q-revolutionen-28#question: Which body directed the Reign of Terror in France in 1793–94?
q-revolutionen-28#explanation: Under Robespierre's leadership the Committee of Public Safety had about 17,000 people executed by revolutionary tribunals, until Robespierre himself was overthrown in July 1794.
q-revolutionen-29#choices.1: Nobles who fled abroad from the Revolution
q-revolutionen-29#choices.2: Priests who refused the oath to the constitution
q-revolutionen-29#explanation: The name means "without knee breeches": they wore long trousers instead of the culottes of the upper classes. They drove the Revolution forward in the streets but under the Constitution of 1791 many were excluded from voting as "passive citizens".
q-revolutionen-30#question: Which country decreed the “levée en masse” in 1793, calling up all men fit for service?
q-revolutionen-30#explanation: The Republic sent hundreds of thousands of young men against the allied monarchies; a formal conscription law followed in 1798. Prussia did not introduce universal conscription until 1814.
q-revolutionen-31#question: Which song became the anthem of the revolutionary movement in the French Revolution and is France's national anthem today?
q-revolutionen-31#explanation: The war song, written in 1792, was carried to Paris by volunteers from Marseille, which gave it its name.
q-revolutionen-32#question: Who reintroduced slavery in the French colonies in 1802?
q-revolutionen-32#explanation: The National Convention had abolished slavery in 1794. Its reintroduction reignited the struggle for freedom in Saint-Domingue, which became independent as Haiti in 1804.
q-revolutionen-33#question: What did the Imperial Recess (Reichsdeputationshauptschluss) of 1803 bring about?
q-revolutionen-33#choices.0: The Holy Roman Empire was declared dissolved
q-revolutionen-33#choices.1: The ecclesiastical principalities and most imperial cities were dissolved
q-revolutionen-33#choices.3: The Prussian peasants were freed from hereditary serfdom
q-revolutionen-33#explanation: Their territories went to larger states such as Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden, which were thus compensated for their losses west of the Rhine.
q-revolutionen-34#question: Which office did Napoleon take up after his coup of 1799?
q-revolutionen-34#explanation: As First Consul he had himself confirmed by a plebiscite and ruled practically alone. In 1804 he made himself Emperor of the French.
q-revolutionen-35#question: Who placed the crown on Napoleon's head at his imperial coronation in Notre-Dame in 1804?
q-revolutionen-35#explanation: The pope was present, but Napoleon placed the crown on his own head to show that he owed his power to no one. He then crowned Joséphine.
q-revolutionen-36#question: On which island was Napoleon Bonaparte born?
q-revolutionen-36#explanation: He was born in Ajaccio in 1769, shortly after France had acquired Corsica from Genoa. He later spent his first exile on Elba.
q-revolutionen-37#question: Which battle of 1805 is also known as the Battle of the Three Emperors?
q-revolutionen-37#explanation: At Austerlitz in Moravia, Emperor Napoleon defeated the armies of the Austrian Emperor Francis and the Russian Tsar Alexander I. He then reorganized Germany according to his will.
q-revolutionen-38#question: Which painter captured the shooting of Madrid insurgents by French soldiers in May 1808 in a famous picture?
q-revolutionen-38#explanation: His painting The Third of May 1808 shows the execution of Madrid citizens after their uprising against the French occupation and is regarded as one of the first modern anti-war pictures.
q-revolutionen-39#question: Why did Napoleon invade Russia in 1812?
q-revolutionen-39#choices.0: Russian troops had occupied allied Prussia
q-revolutionen-39#choices.1: The tsar had promised the Bourbons a return to Paris
q-revolutionen-39#choices.2: Russia had declared war on France beforehand
q-revolutionen-39#choices.3: The tsar had stopped observing the Continental System against Britain
q-revolutionen-39#explanation: The Continental System was meant to cut Britain off from trade with the Continent. When Russia stopped complying, Napoleon marched east with more than 600,000 men.
q-revolutionen-40#question: At which river did Napoleon's Grande Armée finally disintegrate at the end of November 1812?
q-revolutionen-40#explanation: During the crossing of the Berezina on the retreat from Moscow the army fell apart. Of more than 600,000 men, barely more than 50,000 returned.
q-revolutionen-41#question: Which battle in October 1813 went down in history as the Battle of the Nations?
q-revolutionen-41#explanation: Around 600,000 soldiers fought near Leipzig from October 16 to 19. Napoleon then had to retreat across the Rhine and lost control of Germany.
q-revolutionen-42#question: To which island was Napoleon exiled after his defeat at Waterloo?
q-revolutionen-42#explanation: The British took him to the remote Atlantic island of St. Helena, where he died in 1821. He had managed to return from his first exile on Elba in 1815.
q-revolutionen-43#question: How many states made up the German Confederation when it was founded in 1815?
q-revolutionen-43#explanation: The loose confederation, with its Federal Assembly in Frankfurt, replaced the Holy Roman Empire dissolved in 1806; Austria held the presidency.
q-revolutionen-44#question: What did the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 bring about?
q-revolutionen-44#choices.0: The founding of the German Customs Union
q-revolutionen-44#choices.1: The introduction of constitutions in all German states
q-revolutionen-44#choices.2: Press censorship and surveillance of the universities
q-revolutionen-44#choices.3: Prussia joining the Confederation of the Rhine
q-revolutionen-44#explanation: Metternich pushed the decrees through after the writer August von Kotzebue was murdered by a student. The student fraternities (Burschenschaften) were banned.
q-revolutionen-45#question: Which colors did the participants of the Hambach Festival of 1832 carry as a sign of freedom and unity?
q-revolutionen-45#explanation: Around 30,000 people gathered at the castle near Neustadt an der Weinstraße to demand freedom of the press and national unity. Black-red-gold became the national colors in 1848 and 1919.
q-revolutionen-46#question: Which painting became the symbol of the July Revolution of 1830 in Paris?
q-revolutionen-46#explanation: Eugène Delacroix painted Liberty as a female figure carrying the tricolor over the barricades. The revolution toppled Charles X and made Louis-Philippe the Citizen King.
q-revolutionen-47#question: Which country did Queen Marie Antoinette come from?
q-revolutionen-47#explanation: The daughter of Maria Theresa was married to the heir to the French throne at the age of 14. The line attributed to her, that the people should eat cake, is not documented.
q-revolutionen-48#question: From which empire did Greece win its independence in the 1820s?
q-revolutionen-48#explanation: The struggle for freedom from 1821 onward inspired philhellenes all over Europe, including the poet Lord Byron, who died in Greece in 1824.
q-revolutionen-49#question: Which composer struck out the dedication of his Third Symphony to Napoleon when Napoleon made himself emperor?
q-revolutionen-49#explanation: The symphony has been known as the Eroica ever since. Beethoven saw Napoleon's elevation to emperor as a betrayal of the ideals of the Revolution.
q-revolutionen-50#question: Which innovation, still used worldwide today, did revolutionary France introduce?
q-revolutionen-50#choices.0: The division of the earth into time zones
q-revolutionen-50#choices.2: The metric system with the meter and the kilogram
q-revolutionen-50#explanation: Instead of hundreds of regional measures there were to be uniform units derived from nature. The meter was defined as a fraction of the earth's meridian.
q-revolutionen-51#question: What did the Prussian October Edict of 1807 abolish?
q-revolutionen-51#choices.1: The hereditary serfdom of the peasants
q-revolutionen-51#choices.3: The tax exemption of the churches
q-revolutionen-51#explanation: The edict, initiated by Baron vom Stein, began the emancipation of the peasants. Many peasants, however, later had to pay off their obligations by ceding land to the estate owners.
q-revolutionen-52#question: According to which principle did Wilhelm von Humboldt found the university in Berlin in 1810?
q-revolutionen-52#choices.0: Study reserved for sons of the nobility
q-revolutionen-52#choices.1: Training exclusively for the civil service
q-revolutionen-52#choices.2: The unity of research and teaching
q-revolutionen-52#explanation: Professors were to do research and teach their findings at the same time. The Berlin university model became a worldwide example in the 19th century.
q-rom-01#question: In which year was Rome founded according to legend?
q-rom-01#explanation: Roman tradition gives 753 BC as the year of the founding by Romulus.
q-rom-02#question: Against which city did Rome wage the three Punic Wars?
q-rom-02#explanation: Carthage in North Africa was Rome's great rival and was destroyed in 146 BC.
q-rom-03#question: What happened on the Ides of March in 44 BC?
q-rom-03#choices.1: Rome was captured by the Gauls
q-rom-03#explanation: Senators around Brutus and Cassius stabbed Caesar to death on March 15, 44 BC.
q-rom-04#question: What is the form of rule established by Augustus called?
q-rom-04#explanation: Augustus ruled as princeps, the first among equals; hence the Principate.
q-rom-05#question: Which emperor granted the Christians freedom of religion in 313?
q-rom-05#explanation: In 313 Constantine and Licinius agreed in Milan on the free exercise of religion.
q-rom-06#question: Who deposed the last Western Roman emperor in 476?
q-rom-06#explanation: The Germanic commander Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and became king of Italy.
q-rom-07#question: What was the Law of the Twelve Tables of around 450 BC?
q-rom-07#explanation: Under pressure from the plebeians the law was recorded on twelve tables and put on public display in the Forum.
q-rom-08#question: Who led the greatest slave revolt of antiquity from 73 to 71 BC?
q-rom-08#explanation: The gladiator Spartacus escaped from Capua and led tens of thousands of slaves until Crassus defeated him in 71 BC.
q-rom-09#question: Under which emperor did the Roman Empire reach its greatest extent in 117?
q-rom-09#explanation: Trajan conquered Dacia, Armenia and Mesopotamia; his successor Hadrian gave up the eastern conquests again.
q-rom-10#question: What did the Constitutio Antoniniana of the emperor Caracalla lay down in the year 212?
q-rom-10#choices.0: The division of the empire into four parts
q-rom-10#choices.2: The transfer of the capital to Constantinople
q-rom-10#choices.3: Roman citizenship for almost all free inhabitants of the empire
q-rom-10#explanation: The edict made millions of provincial inhabitants Roman citizens; Roman law now applied throughout the empire.
q-rom-11#question: Which form of rule did Diocletian introduce in 293?
q-rom-11#explanation: In the Tetrarchy two emperors and two junior emperors ruled the empire together, in order to defend the frontiers more effectively.
q-rom-12#question: Which scholar was murdered by a Christian mob in Alexandria in 415?
q-rom-12#explanation: The mathematician and philosopher Hypatia became caught up in the power struggle between the city prefect and Bishop Cyril and was killed.
q-rom-13#question: Which Carthaginian general crossed the Alps with elephants in the Second Punic War?
q-rom-13#explanation: Hannibal marched from Spain across the Alps into Italy and was regarded as Rome's most dangerous enemy. Despite great victories he never managed to take Rome.
q-rom-14#question: Whom did Octavian defeat in the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC?
q-rom-14#explanation: After their defeat Antony and Cleopatra fled to Egypt and took their own lives in 30 BC. Egypt then became a Roman province.
q-rom-15#question: Which chieftain of the Cherusci destroyed three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9?
q-rom-15#explanation: Arminius had himself been trained in Roman service and lured the governor Varus into an ambush. Around 15,000 Romans were killed.
q-rom-16#question: Which city was buried under ash when Vesuvius erupted in AD 79?
q-rom-16#explanation: Pompeii was buried together with Herculaneum and thereby preserved. Excavations since the 18th century reveal the everyday life of a Roman town.
q-rom-17#question: Where did Emperor Hadrian have a 118-kilometre frontier wall built from 122 onwards?
q-rom-17#explanation: Hadrian's Wall ran from the North Sea to the Irish Sea. It served less to repel attacks than to control traffic, trade and customs.
q-rom-18#question: Which boundary river did Caesar cross in 49 BC with the words 'Alea iacta est'?
q-rom-18#explanation: By crossing the Rubicon Caesar led his army into Italy without authority and started the civil war against Pompey. 'Crossing the Rubicon' still means a point of no return.
q-rom-19#question: Which month is named after the first Roman emperor?
q-rom-19#explanation: August bears the honorary name Augustus that Octavian received in 27 BC. July, by contrast, is named after Gaius Julius Caesar.
q-rom-20#question: What were the aristocratic families called with whom the plebeians struggled in the Conflict of the Orders?
q-rom-20#explanation: At first the patricians alone held the offices and priesthoods. Over two centuries the Conflict of the Orders won the plebeians the Twelve Tables, the tribunes and finally access to all offices.
q-rom-21#question: What is meant by the phrase 'bread and circuses'?
q-rom-21#choices.0: Soldiers were paid in bread and given games as leave
q-rom-21#choices.1: Bakers and gladiators formed Rome's most important guilds
q-rom-21#choices.2: The emperor could only issue laws at banquets
q-rom-21#choices.3: Free grain and entertainment kept the masses quiet
q-rom-21#explanation: Emperors and politicians won over the people of the capital with grain handouts and games in the Colosseum and Circus Maximus. The phrase goes back to the satirist Juvenal.
q-rom-22#question: What was the Circus Maximus in Rome mainly known for?
q-rom-22#explanation: Hundreds of thousands of spectators cheered on the chariot races in the long racetrack. It thus held many times more people than the Colosseum.
q-rom-23#question: From which province did Rome obtain much of its grain?
q-rom-23#explanation: Grain ships from Egypt and North Africa carried wheat across the Mediterranean to the port of Ostia. The state-organised grain supply fed the city of a million people.
q-rom-24#question: Which of these languages developed from Latin?
q-rom-24#explanation: Like Italian, French, Spanish and Portuguese, Romanian is a Romance language. These languages grew out of the spoken Latin of the provinces.
q-rom-25#question: According to legend, which animal suckled the twins Romulus and Remus?
q-rom-25#explanation: The she-wolf became the emblem of Rome; tradition names Romulus as the city's founder. Archaeologically, the hills by the Tiber were settled from the 10th century BC.
q-rom-26#question: Where did Hannibal win his greatest victory over the Romans in 216 BC?
q-rom-26#explanation: The battle of Cannae is regarded as one of the greatest victories in military history. Hannibal nevertheless lost the war at Zama against Scipio in 202 BC.
q-rom-27#question: What was the consequence of the battle in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 for Rome?
q-rom-27#choices.0: Rome moved its capital to Trier
q-rom-27#choices.1: Rome abandoned the permanent conquest of the land east of the Rhine
q-rom-27#choices.2: Rome made an alliance with all the Germanic tribes
q-rom-27#choices.3: Rome permanently conquered Germania up to the Elbe
q-rom-27#explanation: After the loss of three legions the Rhine and later the limes became the frontier. Germania east of the Rhine remained outside the empire.
q-rom-28#question: Which scholar died in the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79?
q-rom-28#explanation: Pliny the Elder, author of a vast Natural History, died while trying to rescue people on the Bay of Naples. Seneca and Cicero were already dead, and Tacitus lived for decades more.
q-rom-29#question: Which emperor opened the Colosseum in the year 80 with a hundred days of games?
q-rom-29#explanation: His father Vespasian had begun construction in 72; Titus completed and opened it. The amphitheatre held around 50,000 spectators.
q-rom-30#question: What did the tribune Tiberius Gracchus try to push through in 133 BC?
q-rom-30#choices.2: The distribution of public land to impoverished farmers
q-rom-30#explanation: His land reform was meant to save the basis of the citizen army, but he was beaten to death by opponents from the Senate. This violence is seen as the start of the crisis of the Republic.
q-rom-31#question: Cleopatra VII was the last ruler of which dynasty in Egypt?
q-rom-31#explanation: The Ptolemies had ruled Egypt since Alexander's death; Cleopatra was the first of them to speak Egyptian. After her death in 30 BC the country became a Roman province.
q-rom-32#question: Whom did Nero blame for the great fire of Rome in 64?
q-rom-32#explanation: Nero, who was himself suspected of arson, had the Christians cruelly executed. On the ruins he built his palace, the Domus Aurea.
q-rom-33#question: Which school of philosophy did Emperor Marcus Aurelius follow in his Meditations?
q-rom-33#explanation: Marcus Aurelius wrote down his thoughts on duty, transience and composure in Greek while on campaign on the Danube. Seneca was another well-known Roman Stoic.
q-rom-34#question: Which city temporarily broke away from the empire under Queen Zenobia during the crisis of the 3rd century?
q-rom-34#explanation: The Syrian oasis city of Palmyra built up its own realm under Zenobia, reaching as far as Egypt. Emperor Aurelian subdued it and reunited the empire between 270 and 275.
q-rom-35#question: How did Diocletian try to halt rising prices across the empire in 301?
q-rom-35#choices.0: With an edict setting maximum prices
q-rom-35#explanation: The Edict on Maximum Prices set upper limits for goods and wages but was largely ineffective. Diocletian also tied farmers and craftsmen to their occupations.
q-rom-36#question: Which Roman god without a Greek counterpart was depicted with two faces?
q-rom-36#explanation: Janus was the god of gates, passages and beginnings, looking both forwards and backwards. The month of January is named after him.
q-rom-37#question: Which rights did women have in ancient Rome?
q-rom-37#choices.1: They could vote in the Senate
q-rom-37#choices.2: They could own property and get divorced
q-rom-37#explanation: Political office remained closed to women, but they could hold property and divorce. At the imperial court women such as Livia and Agrippina wielded great influence.
q-rom-38#question: Which building material made the huge dome of the Pantheon in Rome possible?
q-rom-38#explanation: Roman concrete was easy to shape and even set under water. It allowed domes, vaults and harbour works that had not been possible before.
q-rom-39#explanation: Carthage was destroyed in 146 BC, Spartacus' revolt followed in 73–71 BC, Caesar was killed in 44 and Actium was fought in 31 BC. With Carthage gone, Rome had lost its greatest rival in the western Mediterranean.
q-rom-40#question: Which admiral led Octavian's fleet to victory at Actium in 31 BC?
q-rom-40#explanation: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa was Octavian's closest commander and cut off Antony's heavy ships. Maecenas, by contrast, was famous as a patron of poets.
q-rom-41#question: Where does the Colosseum get its name from?
q-rom-41#choices.0: From a colossal statue of Nero nearby
q-rom-41#choices.1: From the name of its architect, Colossus
q-rom-41#choices.2: From the town of Colossae in Asia Minor
q-rom-41#choices.3: From the Latin word for gladiator
q-rom-41#explanation: The building was originally called the Flavian Amphitheatre; it only got the name Colosseum in the Middle Ages. It stood on the site of the artificial lake of Nero's palace.
q-rom-42#question: What was found at the fort of Vindolanda on Hadrian's Wall?
q-rom-42#choices.0: The oldest hoard of Roman gold coins
q-rom-42#choices.2: Wooden tablets with letters and shopping lists
q-rom-42#explanation: The tablets, including a birthday invitation, offer a unique glimpse of everyday life on the frontier. Around 10,000 soldiers from all parts of the empire served on the Wall.
q-rom-43#question: Whose conspiracy did Cicero expose as consul in 63 BC?
q-rom-43#explanation: Cicero delivered four famous speeches against Catiline before the Senate and the people and had fellow conspirators executed. After Caesar's death he opposed Mark Antony and was murdered in 43 BC.
q-rom-44#question: Which later emperor was Livia's son from her first marriage?
q-rom-44#explanation: Livia secured Tiberius as successor to her second husband Augustus. Claudius was her grandson and had her deified in 42.
q-rom-45#question: Which Roman emperor was taken prisoner by the Persian king Shapur I in 260?
q-rom-45#explanation: Valerian's capture was a low point of the crisis of the 3rd century. The Sasanian Shapur had his triumph immortalised in rock reliefs.
q-rom-46#question: Where did Diocletian retire after his voluntary abdication in 305?
q-rom-46#explanation: Diocletian was the only emperor to step down voluntarily. The walls of his palace on the Dalmatian coast still enclose the old town of Split today.
q-rom-47#question: Whose teaching did the Council of Nicaea condemn in 325?
q-rom-47#explanation: Arius regarded Christ as a creature of God, whereas the council declared him to be of one substance with the Father. Many Germanic peoples nevertheless later adopted Christianity in its Arian form.
q-rom-48#question: Which Roman general stopped the Hunnic king Attila on the Catalaunian Plains in 451?
q-rom-48#explanation: Aetius had allied himself with the Visigothic king Theodoric I, who fell in the battle. Attila withdrew and died in 453, after which his empire fell apart.
q-rom-49#question: Which work did Augustine write in response to the sack of Rome in 410?
q-rom-49#explanation: Pagans blamed the abandonment of the old gods for the fall of Rome; Augustine contrasted the earthly city with the eternal City of God. He had written his Confessions years earlier.
q-rom-50#question: What were the dependent farmers of late antiquity, bound to their estates, called?
q-rom-50#explanation: The coloni were not allowed to leave the land they farmed. They were forerunners of the dependent peasants of the Middle Ages.
q-rom-51#question: How did the army reform of Marius change the Roman army?
q-rom-51#choices.0: Legionaries became professional soldiers tied to their generals
q-rom-51#choices.1: The army consisted only of cavalry
q-rom-51#choices.2: Only patricians were allowed to serve as soldiers
q-rom-51#choices.3: The legions were placed directly under the Senate
q-rom-51#explanation: From Marius onwards propertyless citizens were also recruited; they served for many years and then expected land or money from their general. Sulla, Pompey and Caesar exploited this loyalty in the civil wars.
q-rom-52#question: What was the name of Rome's last king, whose expulsion around 509 BC led to the Republic?
q-rom-52#explanation: After Tarquinius was driven out, two annually elected consuls took over the government. His epithet Superbus means 'the Proud'.
q-urgeschichte-01#question: On which continent did modern humans, Homo sapiens, emerge?
q-urgeschichte-01#explanation: The oldest fossils of Homo sapiens come from Africa and are around 300,000 years old.
q-urgeschichte-02#question: What is meant by the Neolithic Revolution?
q-urgeschichte-02#choices.0: The transition to farming, animal husbandry and settled life
q-urgeschichte-02#choices.2: The migration of humans out of Africa
q-urgeschichte-02#explanation: In the Neolithic, people began to cultivate plants and breed animals, and lived permanently in villages.
q-urgeschichte-03#question: What is the cave of Lascaux in France known for?
q-urgeschichte-03#choices.1: For Ice Age paintings of animals
q-urgeschichte-03#choices.2: For the skeleton of a Neanderthal
q-urgeschichte-03#choices.3: For the first finds of grain
q-urgeschichte-03#explanation: At Lascaux, people painted hundreds of horses, aurochs and deer on the cave walls about 17,000 years ago.
q-urgeschichte-04#question: How did the first humans reach America?
q-urgeschichte-04#choices.1: Over a land bridge from Africa
q-urgeschichte-04#choices.3: Over the Bering land bridge from Siberia to Alaska
q-urgeschichte-04#explanation: During the Ice Age the sea level was so low that there was solid land between Siberia and Alaska.
q-urgeschichte-05#question: How did Ötzi, the Iceman, die?
q-urgeschichte-05#choices.0: From a fall into a crevasse
q-urgeschichte-05#choices.2: From freezing to death in a snowstorm
q-urgeschichte-05#explanation: An arrowhead in his left shoulder shows that Ötzi was killed.
q-urgeschichte-06#question: What is remarkable about Göbekli Tepe in present-day Turkey?
q-urgeschichte-06#choices.0: It is the oldest city with a city wall
q-urgeschichte-06#choices.2: Monumental stone circles were erected there while people were still hunters and gatherers
q-urgeschichte-06#choices.3: The oldest cuneiform tablets were found there
q-urgeschichte-06#explanation: The T-shaped pillars of Göbekli Tepe were created around 9500 BC, before farming and animal husbandry had taken hold in the region.
q-urgeschichte-07#question: Which human species was the first to leave Africa and spread as far as Java and China?
q-urgeschichte-07#explanation: Homo erectus reached the Caucasus about 1.8 million years ago and later East and Southeast Asia.
q-urgeschichte-08#question: Where were the oldest known clay vessels in the world made?
q-urgeschichte-08#explanation: Sherds from the Xianrendong Cave in southern China are around 18,000 to 20,000 years old and still come from hunters and gatherers.
q-urgeschichte-09#question: What is the Blombos Cave in South Africa known for?
q-urgeschichte-09#choices.2: For the oldest engraved patterns and ornamental beads
q-urgeschichte-09#choices.3: For the first finds of grain
q-urgeschichte-09#explanation: In the Blombos Cave, pieces of ochre around 75,000 years old bearing geometric patterns and pierced snail shells were found.
q-urgeschichte-10#choices.0: Through a complete skeleton in Siberia
q-urgeschichte-10#choices.1: Through cave paintings in the Altai
q-urgeschichte-10#choices.3: Through DNA analysis of a finger bone
q-urgeschichte-10#explanation: In 2010 the genome of a previously unknown human species was obtained from a tiny finger bone from the Denisova Cave.
q-urgeschichte-11#question: Which settlement in the Jordan Valley was given a stone wall and a tower around 8000 BC?
q-urgeschichte-11#explanation: Jericho is regarded as one of the oldest permanently inhabited settlements in the world; the tower is almost nine meters high.
q-urgeschichte-12#question: By what do archaeologists recognize the seafarers who settled the Pacific islands from about 1500 BC onward?
q-urgeschichte-12#explanation: The Lapita culture is named after a site in New Caledonia; its characteristically decorated pottery marks the path of settlement as far as Tonga and Samoa.
q-urgeschichte-13#question: What separates prehistory from later history?
q-urgeschichte-13#choices.0: It is the time before the invention of writing
q-urgeschichte-13#choices.1: It is the time before the use of fire
q-urgeschichte-13#choices.2: It is the time before farming
q-urgeschichte-13#choices.3: It is the time before the first metalworking
q-urgeschichte-13#explanation: There are no written sources for prehistory; it is reconstructed from bones, tools, cave art, settlement remains and ancient DNA.
q-urgeschichte-14#question: To which species does the famous fossil 'Lucy' belong?
q-urgeschichte-14#explanation: Lucy was found in 1974 at Hadar in Ethiopia; about 40 percent of her roughly 3.2-million-year-old skeleton survives.
q-urgeschichte-15#question: What does Lucy's skeleton reveal about human evolution?
q-urgeschichte-15#choices.0: The large brain arose long before upright walking
q-urgeschichte-15#choices.3: Upright walking arose long before the large brain
q-urgeschichte-15#explanation: Lucy already walked upright on two legs but still had a small brain; she was only about 1.05 metres tall.
q-urgeschichte-16#question: Which stone tool is typical of Homo erectus?
q-urgeschichte-16#explanation: The almond-shaped hand axe, worked on both sides, was used for cutting, scraping and chopping and stayed in use for over a million years.
q-urgeschichte-17#question: In which present-day country is Dmanisi, where skulls of Homo erectus about 1.8 million years old were found?
q-urgeschichte-17#explanation: The finds from Dmanisi in the Caucasus show how early Homo erectus left Africa; later it reached Java and China.
q-urgeschichte-18#question: What is the so-called Turkana Boy?
q-urgeschichte-18#choices.0: The child skeleton of a Neanderthal from France
q-urgeschichte-18#choices.1: An almost complete skeleton of a young Homo erectus from Kenya
q-urgeschichte-18#choices.2: The oldest skull of a Homo sapiens from Morocco
q-urgeschichte-18#choices.3: The child skeleton of a Homo floresiensis from Indonesia
q-urgeschichte-18#explanation: The roughly 1.6-million-year-old skeleton from Lake Turkana is the best-known fossil of Homo erectus and shows its human-like build with long legs.
q-urgeschichte-19#question: Since when at the latest have humans used fire regularly?
q-urgeschichte-19#explanation: Hearths in Africa, Israel and Europe attest to its regular use; fire gave warmth, kept predators away and made cooked food richer in energy.
q-urgeschichte-20#question: In which present-day country were the oldest known fossils of Homo sapiens found?
q-urgeschichte-20#explanation: The finds from Jebel Irhoud are around 300,000 years old, older than the previously known fossils of modern humans from East Africa.
